### H-464 · A client that sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip` was asked about at the main installation on every artifact read, cause not found

Stage: R-BAS-022, a read of a cached artifact. Subject: the load on the main installation, not a confidentiality property.

Observed once by the end-to-end run (`TestBastion_R_BAS_049_RoutingByPath` before it used `curl` from a client pod): 36 tarballs requested twice by the Go client of the test
machine, which sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip` by default, caused 72 conditional requests (every one answered `304`) and no hit, on the volume Bastion, while the same paths requested
without that header by `curl` caused one conditional request per stale path and hits afterwards (a probe of one path, and a loop of 20 requests, checked in the cluster). The package
managers of the suite (npm, pnpm, Yarn 4, `dotnet restore`) were served from the cache as the acceptance requires. The cache key carries the values of the headers the main
installation's `Vary` names (R-BAS-018); the cause is probably a variant that is keyed by `Accept-Encoding` and never becomes fresh, and it was not found. Live for a client that sends the header
and reads a cached artifact: it costs the main installation one conditional request per read, never the bytes. What makes it real: a client built on a library that compresses by default
and reads the same artifacts many times; the Bastion's concurrency budget (R-BAS-025) bounds what reaches the main installation.

### H-1102 · The Bastion serves what it cached for up to ten minutes after the switch is turned on

Stage: R-BAS-022, a read of a cached artifact; the switch of [malware-scanning.md](malware-scanning.md) R-MAL-019. Subject: callers of a
Bastion after an administrator turned on **Only checked artifacts can be downloaded**, or a repository's stricter setting (R-MAL-020).
Specified, not built. The switch makes `pending`, `unscannable` and `failed` content unservable at the main installation, and no feed entry
carries that change ([Q-BAS-164](#q-bas-164--the-malware-scannings-events-in-the-feed-a-find-and-a-withdrawn-release-are-content)): an
artifact the Bastion cached before stays servable from its cache until its next revalidation, at most `artifact_revalidate_after`
(10 minutes by default), as [H-385](#h-385--a-withdrawal-the-feed-does-not-carry-reaches-the-bastion-within-the-artifact-revalidation-period)
says of the withdrawals the feed does not carry. A find (`malware.found`) and a withdrawn release reach it through the feed within seconds.
What makes it real: content that was served before the switch, read through a Bastion in the minutes after it.

### H-1242 · Every pull with a registry token costs the main installation its token request and one check

Stage: R-BAS-052, R-BAS-022 and R-BAS-085, a cached image read with a registry token. Subject: the request load on the main installation
and the miss limit of the caller's address (R-BAS-035), not a confidentiality property.

Live for every image pulled through a Bastion with a registry token, which is almost every pull. A client takes a new registry token for
each pull, and a new token is a stranger to the Bastion. *As built on 2026-11-23* (R-BAS-084, R-BAS-085,
[Q-BAS-167](#q-bas-167--a-registry-token-is-checked-by-the-main-installation-and-its-read-shape-is-at-most-partial) option (b)): the token
is `full` on the images of its grant, so its first read of the pull costs one request, a check or the forward whose marking gives the
package answer, and the rest of the pull is served from the cache; until then it cost one conditional request per manifest and blob. Each
request is a miss of the address. Measured with an image of ten layers
([developer/bastion.md](../developer/bastion.md#the-real-clients-through-a-bastion)): a warm pull costs Docker 29.9.3 4 requests (the probe
and the token, its anonymous `HEAD` of the tag while the main installation admits anonymous reads,
[H-1420](#h-1420--while-the-main-installation-admits-anonymous-reads-a-clients-first-head-of-a-tag-without-a-credential-is-forwarded-on-every-pull),
and the forwarded `HEAD` of the tag, which has no entry because Docker never `GET`s it), Podman 5.8.9 2 (the token and a check, or the tag's
forward), containerd 2.3.4 through crictl 5 to 6 (two probes, two tokens, a check per token), instead of 13 to 19 before. The miss limit of
one address (4,000 a minute with a credential since R-BAS-092, 300 before) is then reached at about 1,000 Docker pulls, 2,000 Podman pulls or 650 to 800 containerd pulls a minute (at 300: 75, 150 and 50 to 60, instead of 16 to
23). What makes it real: many nodes behind one address pulling at once (a rollout through a NAT), which reaches the miss limit
(`429 TOOMANYREQUESTS`, which clients retry), or a main installation for which these requests matter. What would close more, outside the
design of R-BAS-080 to R-BAS-088: keeping a `204 read-with-body` probe answer of `POST /v2/_token` as the `403` and `404` probe answers
are kept (one request less per Docker pull, two per containerd pull), closing H-1420 (one less per Docker pull while anonymous reads are on),
and answers carried in the token service's answer ([Q-BAS-245](#q-bas-245--when-the-bastion-asks) option (d)); meanwhile
`bastion.blocking.exempt_cidrs` or a higher miss limit for such an address.

### H-1243 · A plain index path of a Debian remote without by-hash can disagree with the InRelease a Bastion serves

Stage: R-BAS-055, documents of the metadata period. Subject: an `apt update` through a Bastion of a remote repository whose upstream does
not announce `Acquire-By-Hash`, and of a flat repository (Q-DEB-23).

Live for such repositories only: every release Quader writes, and the Debian and Ubuntu archives, announce by-hash. The Bastion keeps the `InRelease` and the plain path of each index as separate documents, each revalidated after
`metadata_revalidate_after`; when the upstream publishes in between, a client can read an `InRelease` of one generation and an index of
another, and APT refuses the index with "Hash Sum mismatch" and keeps its previous list until its next update. The main installation
has the same race between two requests, for the time between them; the Bastion widens it to the period (1 minute by default). What
makes it real: an `apt update` through a Bastion within a period after such an upstream published. What closes it: revalidating the
release documents on every request (Q-BAS-174 option (b)).

### H-1244 · Cold fills of large blobs hold budget slots and spool for the length of their transfer

Stage: R-BAS-054, R-BAS-025, R-BAS-030. Subject: the availability of misses at the Bastion for other callers.

Live wherever large layers are readable through a Bastion, and anonymously where they are `public`. A fill holds
its budget slot until the main installation's body ends and its bytes in the spool until it commits; a layer of 2 GiB at 100 MB/s holds
both for about twenty seconds. Sixteen anonymous requests for distinct cold layers hold the anonymous share of the default budget
(64 slots, a quarter), and the spool of 2 GiB holds one such layer, so a further cold layer is passed through unkept
([H-450](#h-450--a-fill-that-does-not-fit-the-spool-is-passed-through-unkept-and-a-request-answered-from-the-spool-fails)).
What bounds it: the per-address request and miss limits, `max_object_bytes`, and the 60 s without a byte after which a fill is
abandoned. What makes it real: an attacker below the limits, from several addresses, naming distinct large layers that exist; [H-472](#h-472--a-fill-goes-on-after-its-client-has-left)
says that it need not wait for them. Narrowed by the handover (R-BAS-074): a fill read from the object store frees its budget slot with the
handover's answer, so where a registration's handover is on, such fills hold the spool and no slot; the spool's part stays.

*Revised on 2026-11-26 by the owner's [Q-BAS-331](#q-bas-331--the-maximum-throughput-is-enforced-at-the-bastion-on-every-byte-it-reads):* the throughput paces fills (R-BAS-097), so at the cap a cold fill
holds its slot and its spool longer than the figures above; the cap bounds the bytes, the slots still bound the fills in flight. *Since E10
(2026-11-26)* the cap holds: at the default 200 MB/s a cold fill of 2 GiB holds its slot at least 11 s, and while transfers share the cap
each holds it longer.

### H-1245 · A caller on another replica waits for a running fill without a byte up to fill_wait_max

Stage: R-BAS-054, the fetch lock across replicas (the bucket backend with Valkey). Subject: the time to the first byte of a large
layer for callers whose request reaches another replica than the fill.

Live on a Bastion with the bucket backend, Valkey and several replicas, where requests are spread without routing by path. The spool of a fill is local to its replica, so a caller on another replica cannot follow it: it waits, without a
byte, until the fill commits or `fill_wait_max` (10 minutes by default) passes, and then fetches itself. A client with a timeout for
the first byte below the fill's time gives up and retries, which keeps it waiting. What makes it real: a client of a large cold layer
with such a timeout, on another replica than the fill. The volume backend with routing by path (R-BAS-033) brings every caller of a path
to one replica.

### H-1246 · A compromised Bastion can serve an older genuine document of a repository

Stage: R-BAS-055 and R-BAS-053, what a Bastion keeps of signed indexes and of tags. Subject: the freshness of what a client installs:
security fixes, a moved tag, a withdrawn package's absence from an index.

Dormant while no Bastion is taken over; live for a Bastion pod in an attacker's hands (or the signing key with write access to its
cache, [H-387](#h-387--the-signing-key-and-write-access-to-the-bastions-valkey-or-bucket-together-forge-answers-and-entries)). A signed
`InRelease` cannot be forged at a Bastion, but an older one can be served again: a local or virtual repository's release carries no
`Valid-Until` ([formats/debian.md](formats/debian.md#h-624--quaders-own-release-files-carry-no-valid-until) H-624), so APT accepts it
for as long as it is served, and a tag's earlier manifest is accepted by every image client, which verifies a digest and not the
age of a tag. The same holds for npm's and NuGet's documents. What makes it real: a taken-over Bastion pod serving the clients that
trust it. What narrows it: `Valid-Until` on Quader's own releases (Debian's deferred table), and pulls by digest.

### H-1247 · The certificate admission of the ClamAV definitions does not reach a Bastion

Stage: R-BAS-056, Q-BAS-176. Subject: a ClamAV installation outside the company that is admitted by its client certificate only.

Dormant: a limit of the design, not a weakness. A Bastion serves the ClamAV definitions to the anonymous caller and to tokens; an
installation that has no token and whose repository level is below `public` reaches the main installation's certificate endpoint, which
must then be reachable from where it runs. What makes it real: a company that keeps the definitions at `internal` and wants its
external ClamAV installations admitted by certificate through a Bastion.

### H-1248 · A binding changed at the main installation reaches a Bastion at its next handshake

Stage: R-BAS-057, the bound repository of a Bastion's host. Subject: what a Bastion of a bound host keys its answers and entries by.

Dormant until a main installation binds a Bastion's host (the Bastion's side of R-BAS-057 is built). The Bastion learns `boundRepository` at the handshake (every
`bastion.main.handshake_interval`); a binding changed at the main installation in between makes the Bastion key `/v2/<name>/…` by the
old repository while the main installation serves the new one. A forward and a conditional request are decided by the main installation
on the new binding, so nothing is read that the caller may not read; a `full` answer and a cached entry of the old repository can serve
the old repository's bytes to a caller who reads it in full until the next handshake. What makes it real: an administrator who moves a
bound host to another repository while clients pull through the Bastion. What closes it: a `settings` feed entry for a change of
`host_roots`, which is configuration and journals nothing today.

### H-1249 · Five documents of npm and OCI carry no validator, so a Bastion fetches them whole once per metadata period

Stage: R-BAS-023, the revalidation of a shared document, for npm's routes `npm.root`, `npm.disttags.get`, `npm.keys.get` and
`npm.attestations.get` and OCI's `oci.tags.list`. Subject: the request and transfer load on the main installation, not a confidentiality
property.

Live on every Bastion that serves npm or OCI (the registry root is served, R-BAS-051). Kit check 19 found that these routes answer
without an `ETag` (R-BAS-058, [Q-BAS-184](#q-bas-184--kit-check-19-judges-what-a-bastion-keeps-and-a-route-is-exempt-from-two-duties-only-with-a-reason));
their fixtures list them in `NoBastion` with this gap as the reason. A Bastion keeps such a document as any other, but its revalidation
after `metadata_revalidate_after` cannot be conditional, so the main installation renders and sends the whole document again: a few
hundred bytes for the root, the dist-tags and the keys, a few KiB for the attestations of a version, and up to a page of 1,000 names for a
tags list. The cost is one transfer per document, period and replica, not per caller. What makes it real: many repositories of these
formats read through a Bastion, where the documents add up. What closes it: an `ETag` and an answer of `If-None-Match` with `304` in each
of the five handlers, after which their `NoBastion` entries are removed and check 19 holds them.

### H-1290 · A miss passed through during an outage of the object store is marked as counted

Stage: R-BAS-059, the counted note at the status line of the remote engine's artifact answer (Q-BAS-186). Subject: the main
installation's audit trail of the downloads a Bastion serves from its cache.

Live while the main installation's object store is unavailable: the Bastion's side reports counted entries (R-BAS-059). The remote
engine streams a miss to the first caller and writes its status line before the commit; when the commit finds the object store
unavailable, the body is passed through, not stored and not counted (`passThrough` in [artifact.go](../../internal/proxy/artifact.go)),
yet the answer carries `Quader-Bastion-Counted`. A Bastion that keeps the answer reports its later hits as downloads of a fill the main
installation recorded none for. It over-reports and hands no caller anything its own permission does not cover. What makes it real: an
outage of the object store during a cold fill through a Bastion, and an answer whose `ETag` is a content address, which the Bastion keeps.

### H-1296 · A freshclam run through a Bastion asks the main installation once per database for the .cld it never serves

Stage: R-BAS-056, R-BAS-024. Subject: the request load on the main installation, not a confidentiality property.

Live wherever ClamAV installations update through a Bastion. `freshclam` 1.5.5 asks for `<db>.cld` before `<db>.cvd`; the endpoint serves
signed containers only and answers `404` from the format's handler (`container` in
[handlers.go](../../internal/formats/clamav/handlers.go)), which notes no missing item, so the marking says `pass`, not `absent`, and the
Bastion forwards each of the three requests of every run (measured on 2026-11-22, [developer/bastion.md](../developer/bastion.md#the-real-clients-through-a-bastion)).
What makes it real: many ClamAV installations behind one Bastion, each checking every hour or more often. What closes it: the
format's `404` for a database file it never serves noted as missing (`bastionmain.NoteMissing`), so a full reader's Bastion keeps the
negative entry for `negative_period`.

### H-1325 · A change of the cache key loses the download events spooled under the old layout

Stage: R-BAS-039's audit spool and R-BAS-061. Subject: the download events of cached hits, which reach the main installation's audit trail.

Live during a rollout that changes, sets or removes `secrets.cacheKey` while the main installation cannot be reached. A draining replica of the
old configuration writes the events it could not send to the audit spool in its own layout; a replica of the new one cannot read a tree of
another key, and with a key it delivers no plain spool file, because whoever can write the cache store could have written one (Q-BAS-213).
The sweep of other layouts then deletes them (Q-BAS-215). What makes it real: an outage of the main installation during such a rollout; the
lost events are missing from the audit as those of [H-391](#h-391--download-events-lost-to-a-full-buffer-a-crash-or-an-ephemeral-spool-are-missing-from-the-audit)
are. A key change while the main installation is reachable loses nothing.

### H-1326 · After a key change the old tree stays readable to a holder of the old key until the sweep has deleted it

Stage: R-BAS-061, the sweep of other layouts
([Q-BAS-215](#q-bas-215--the-sweep-of-other-layouts-deletes-them-in-a-replicas-first-hour-and-while-it-still-finds-some)). Subject: what
the old tree holds.

Live after every change of the cache key; it matters when the key was changed because it leaked. A new key protects nothing already written:
the old tree stays in the cache store until the replicas of the new key have deleted it, at most 10,000 objects per sweep (one sweep every
`sweep_interval`, 5 minutes by default), during each replica's first hour and as long as a sweep still finds some; with the bucket backend and
Valkey one replica sweeps. A replica of the old key that still writes after the first hour of every new replica (a rollout longer than an
hour, or a second deployment on the same prefix) leaves those objects until the next start. What makes it real: a leaked cache key together
with read access to the cache store. Emptying the prefix at the provider, or the volume, is the operator's faster step.

### H-1327 · A taken-over Bastion pod holds the cache key

Stage: R-BAS-061, the custody of the cache key. Subject: the content of the cache store.

Live wherever a cache key is set. The key is a mounted file of every replica, and the storage key and name key derived from it live in each
replica's memory for its life (Go cannot erase an AES key schedule, as for the main installation's storage keys,
[H-1309](../security/stored-content-keys.md#h-1309--a-replicas-memory-holds-the-storage-keys-for-its-life-and-go-cannot-erase-a-key)).
Whoever runs code in a Bastion pod, or reads its memory or its mounted Secrets, reads and writes the whole cache store as the Bastion does. The
key protects the cache against a holder of the store (the bucket's credential, its provider, a copy or a snapshot of a volume), not against
the pod. What makes it real: a flaw that lets an attacker run code in a Bastion process, which then also holds the callers' credentials in
transit ([H-386](#h-386--whoever-holds-the-bastion-token-can-test-credentials-name-client-addresses-and-add-download-events)).

### H-1380 · Changes the feed does not carry reach registry-token and package-narrowed readers within the revalidation periods, no longer at their next read

Stage: R-BAS-085 and R-BAS-022, a cached entry served on a `full` package answer. Subject: registry tokens and readers narrowed by package,
for content the main installation stopped serving by a change no feed entry carries.

Live since R-BAS-084 and R-BAS-085 were built (2026-11-23) for every image pulled with a registry token and every reader `full` on a
package. Until then such a caller asked the main installation for every cached artifact, so every gate judged every pull. With a package answer it is
served from the cache under the rules of a full reader, and a change the feed does not carry reaches it within `artifact_revalidate_after`
(10 minutes) for artifacts and `metadata_revalidate_after` (1 minute) for documents, as
[H-385](#h-385--a-withdrawal-the-feed-does-not-carry-reaches-the-bastion-within-the-artifact-revalidation-period) and
[H-1102](#h-1102--the-bastion-serves-what-it-cached-for-up-to-ten-minutes-after-the-switch-is-turned-on) already allow full readers. What
makes it real: an automatic vulnerability block, the malware scanning's switch turned on, or an upstream withdrawal during a rollout that
pulls through a Bastion. What narrows it: shorter periods, and a transactional event for automatic blocks, which would put that case into
the feed.

### H-1381 · The main installation's limits and blocks do not reach hits from per-package answers

Stage: R-BAS-084 and R-BAS-085; [usage-and-limits.md](usage-and-limits.md) R-LIM-001 and R-LIM-025. Subject: a subject at its request
figures, or blocked, that reads through a Bastion.

Live since R-BAS-084 and R-BAS-085 were built (2026-11-23). Hits are charged nowhere (R-LIM-001, "Later"), so a subject at its request
figures or blocked (R-LIM-025) keeps reading warm content through a Bastion while its package answer is usable. **Without end, as built**
([Q-BAS-270](#q-bas-270--a-package-answer-that-ended-with-its-shape-answer-is-renewed-by-the-check)): a package answer ends together with the
shape answer it was obtained with, so the next read is the check of R-BAS-085 step 4 and not a conditional request, and the check consults
no limit, so it renews both; the conditional request that would meet the limits comes only while the shape answer outlives the package
answer. The same holds for a full reader, whose shape answer the background refresh renews through the check (`refreshShape` in
[background.go](../../internal/bastion/engine/background.go); [bastion_check_api.go](../../internal/api/v1/bastion_check_api.go)), read in the
code and not run. What makes it real: a blocked or limited subject with a usable answer at a Bastion. What would close it: the check
consulting the subject's block and request figures, which closes both cases.

### H-1382 · Whoever holds the Bastion token learns a held credential's shape per package

Stage: the check of R-BAS-083. Subject: the read rights of a credential the holder of the Bastion token already holds; it widens
[H-386](#h-386--whoever-holds-the-bastion-token-can-test-credentials-name-client-addresses-and-add-download-events).

Dormant until a Bastion token leaks (R-BAS-083 is built). The holder can ask the check for any credential it holds about any
(repository, package) pair and learns `full` or `partial` for each. That tells it no more than requesting content with that credential
would, and it cannot make the main installation mark or decide anything differently. What makes it real: a taken-over Bastion pod or a
leaked Secret; revoking the token ends it.

### H-1383 · Per-package sharing rests on the core's notes and kit check 21

Stage: R-BAS-081, R-BAS-082 and R-BAS-086, the package of a response and the class `shared` for a reader of one package. Subject: the
documents of packages a reader of one package may not read.

Dormant: once built, every format passes check 21. What makes it real: a route of a format that decides another package after its status
line, or that lists other packages without a package-less decision, together with a fixture whose cases or second package do not exercise
it. A response the main installation renders for a reader of the whole repository could then be marked with one package and shared with a
reader of only that package. What holds it: kit check 21 over every content case with a second package seeded, and its two `testformat`
defects.

### H-1384 · The first read of a cached entry by a credential without a shape answer costs two requests, an uncached one costs one

Stage: R-BAS-022, the read flow for a credential the Bastion has no shape answer for. Subject: whether a path hidden from a narrowed reader
is cached at the Bastion.

**A finding about today's code, read and not run** ([readflow.go](../../internal/bastion/engine/readflow.go), lines 92 to 105),
present today and not widened by R-BAS-080 to R-BAS-088. A credential without a shape answer that reads a cached entry costs a check and
then a conditional request; one that reads an uncached path costs one forward. A narrowed reader with a fresh credential can therefore tell
a cached hidden path from a missing one by timing, and registry tokens make fresh credentials cheap. This undermines what
[Q-BAS-124](#q-bas-124--a-404-that-is-not-marked-absent-is-never-kept-as-a-url-answer) aims for. R-BAS-085 step 5 does not add the same
signal per package, because a caller with a known `partial` shape gets the conditional request without a check (as built on 2026-11-23,
`TestR_BAS_085_NoRoundTripTellsACachedPackageFromAnUncachedOne`). What makes it real: a
narrowed reader with fresh registry tokens timing first reads of hidden paths. What would close it, a separate decision: answering the
first read with the conditional request and learning a `none` shape in the background.

### H-1390 · Kit check 21 runs over the local class only

Stage: R-BAS-086, the format contract that the package of a response rests on (R-BAS-081). Subject: the documents of packages a reader of one
package may not read, served by a remote or a virtual repository.

Live since the marking per package (R-BAS-082) and the Bastion's sharing per package (R-BAS-085) are built, for every remote and virtual
repository a Bastion serves. Check 21
serves the fixture's content cases on a local host, so it does not run the handlers of the other classes (the remote and virtual handlers
of npm, NuGet, Debian and Ansible Galaxy, OCI's virtual read) nor the routes a fixture lists in `NoContent` (Debian's indexes and by-hash
files, the flat directories, a virtual repository's member paths; NuGet's operations not built; Ansible Galaxy's role routes; npm's audit
and its deferred routes). They were read on 2026-11-22 for a decision after a write (a scan of every handler for a decision after its first
`WriteHeader`, `Write` or `Serve`) and none was found; Debian's indexes decide a package-less read. What makes it real: a remote or virtual
handler that renders a document from another package's data, or decides after its status line, without a local twin that a case reaches.
What would close it: check 21 over the `Remote` and `Merge` fixtures, as check 13 serves them, once the kit's hosts of those classes can
serve a document whole.

### H-1395 · An official image of a Docker Hub remote without a namespace prefix names two packages and carries none

Stage: R-BAS-081 and R-BAS-082, the package of a response through an OCI remote whose upstream is Docker Hub without a namespace prefix.
Subject: the requests a pull of such an image costs the main installation, not what a caller may read.

**Read in the code, not run** ([remote_handlers.go](../../internal/formats/oci/remote_handlers.go), `gateRemote` and `otherSpellingOf`). On
such a remote `nginx` and `library/nginx` are one upstream image, and a read of either is decided twice: `Host.Authorize` on the name the
client sent and `Host.PathsAllowed` on the path of the other spelling, which the format's `Classify` places in the other package. Two
packages are named, so the response carries none (R-BAS-081's rule), and a registry token or a narrowed reader pulling an official image
through such a remote pays a conditional request per artifact, as before R-BAS-080 to R-BAS-088. The rule is right to clear it: the main
installation refuses a reader who may read one spelling and not the other, so a Bastion must not serve that reader on a package answer of
one name. Live since R-BAS-084 and R-BAS-085 were built (2026-11-23) for every official Docker Hub image pulled with a registry token
through such a remote. Images with a namespace (`bitnami/redis`) and remotes with a namespace prefix are not affected. What would close it:
the format naming one canonical package for both spellings in the targets it authorizes, which changes the grants that match today.

### H-1420 · While the main installation admits anonymous reads, a client's first HEAD of a tag without a credential is forwarded on every pull

Stage: R-BAS-019, R-BAS-021 and R-BAS-051, the anonymous caller below `/v2/`; it rests on
[H-442](#h-442--a-401-states-the-subject-as-invalid-whether-the-credential-was-rejected-or-none-was-sent). Subject: the request load on the
main installation and the miss limit of the client's address, not a confidentiality property.

**Found by the measurement of 2026-11-23** ([developer/bastion.md](../developer/bastion.md#the-real-clients-through-a-bastion)), live wherever
the main installation admits anonymous reads (any repository whose artifacts are `public`, so the handshake says `anonymousReads`) and a
client that resolves like containerd pulls a private image through a Bastion: Docker 29.9.3 with its containerd image store sends the
`HEAD` of the tag without a credential first and asks the token service after the challenge. The Bastion admits the anonymous caller,
has no answer for it on the repository and no entry for the tag (Docker never `GET`s it), and forwards the `HEAD`; the main installation's
`401` marks the subject `invalid`, as every `401` does, so the Bastion keeps no answer for the anonymous caller and forwards the next pull's
`HEAD` again: one request and one miss of the address per pull, beside the token step. Without anonymous reads the Bastion answers the
challenge itself. What makes it real: many pulls behind one address against an installation with any public repository. What would close
it: a `401` to a request without a credential marked with the anonymous subject and the shape `none` on the repository, which the Bastion
keeps for `answers.period` and answers the challenge from (H-442's own closing); or a check for the anonymous caller instead of the
forward, which keeps the same answer.

### H-1445 · The store's answers to a Bastion's direct reads are counted only as outcomes

Stage: the link client of R-BAS-074 and the metrics of R-BAS-075. Subject: an operator's view of why handovers fail, not a confidentiality or
integrity property.

Dormant until a main installation hands over (package 2 of [the build plan](../developer/bastion-handover.md)) and a registration's handover
is on. The link client counts no request in the shared outbound metrics (`quader_outbound_requests_total` by purpose and code), because the
outbound factory registers them once per process and the client of the main installation does so first; a second factory on the same registry
would collide. So a store that refuses the links with `403`, one that answers `5xx`, a wrong length and a network that does not reach the store
all show as `quader_bastion_handovers_total{outcome="fallback"}` and the cooldown's gauge; the cause is in the Bastion's log line "a handover is
replaced by the forward without the offer" (level info, field `reason`, never the link). What makes it real: an operator who reads the metrics
and not the logs when `QuaderBastionHandoverFailing` fires. What would close it: one outbound factory shared by the two clients of the Bastion,
so that both count by their purpose.

### H-1480 · The Bastions screen shows what the main installation can sign, not what a Bastion can read

Stage: the card's lines of R-BAS-071 (package 5 of [the build plan](../developer/bastion-handover.md)). Subject: an administrator's view of
whether the direct reads work, not a confidentiality or integrity property.

Dormant until a registration's handover is on. The card names a connection only when the settings' answer says it cannot serve a handover
(R-STOR-096): its address is not `https` or is a host of Quader, or the replica that answered could not read its own link. A connection whose
address the main installation reaches but a Bastion's network does not, whose certificate a Bastion does not trust, or whose host name is
the one a Bastion knows as the main installation's (Q-BAS-281: the main installation does not know a Bastion's `bastion.main.url`) shows
nothing on the card, and every large file of it goes through the main installation after a fallback. What a Bastion met is on the Bastion:
`quader_bastion_handovers_total{outcome}`, the alert `QuaderBastionHandoverFailing` and its log line (R-BAS-075, H-1445), which the main
installation does not receive. What makes it real: an administrator who switches the handover on, sees no line on the card and reads that as
working. The manual says how to see that it works ([admin/bastion.md](../manual/admin/bastion.md#direct-reads-from-the-object-store)), and
the test link is run from the Bastion's network. What would close it: the Bastion's report (R-BAS-059) carrying its outcomes per
connection, which the card would show.

### H-2270 · A replica learns another replica's writes to a shared bucket only at its own listings

Stage: R-BAS-089, the estimate of a replica of the bucket backend
([Q-BAS-302](#q-bas-302--a-replica-on-a-shared-bucket-counts-each-of-its-commits-once-per-replica)). Subject: the size of the Bastion's
bucket, not the availability of a pod.

Live on every Bastion with the bucket backend and more than one replica. A replica counts each of its own commits `bastion.replicas` times and
learns the others' only from its listings, so while the replicas fill evenly its estimate is the bucket's, and when one replica fills more
than its share the bucket can pass `max_bytes` by what that replica wrote beyond its share since another replica's last listing. A bucket has
no fixed size: the excess costs storage until the next sweep evicts it, and no pod is evicted. A replica that fills alone counts its fills
twice with two replicas and lists more often, which costs `ListObjectsV2` requests and no eviction. What makes it real: a release without
routing in which one replica takes most of the cold misses for longer than a sweep interval. What would close it: a counter per area in
Valkey (option (b) of Q-BAS-302).

### H-2271 · A sweep the size asks for costs a listing of the area, at most one a second per replica

Stage: R-BAS-089, the sweeps the size starts
([Q-BAS-303](#q-bas-303--at-once-is-one-sweep-at-a-time-asked-for-by-any-number-of-commits-at-most-one-a-second)). Subject: the requests a
Bastion sends its bucket, and the CPU of a walk of a large volume.

Live on every Bastion; it matters for a bucket of many objects. A sweep lists the area twice and the markers once. While fills arrive faster
than a sweep frees room (a flood of distinct artifacts, H-2272), or the backend fails, a replica sweeps once a second: on a bucket of 18 GiB
of objects of 100 KiB that is about 540 requests of `ListObjectsV2` a second per replica, and fills are passed through unkept between two
sweeps. `quader_bastion_cache_sweeps_total{trigger="size"}` shows it. What makes it real: a sustained churn of distinct artifacts above the
rate one sweep evicts.

### H-2272 · A churn of distinct artifacts still evicts the working set and crosses the transfer network

Stage: R-BAS-031, R-BAS-089 and the fills of R-BAS-021. Subject: the hit rate of legitimate callers and the network between the Bastion and the
main installation, the owner's case of W-34 (2026-11-26).

Live wherever a caller can read more distinct content through a Bastion than its cache holds. R-BAS-089 keeps the cache within its size and
the pod alive, which was the defect; it does not change what is kept. Eviction is by last access, and a fill is an access, so a stream of
single requests for distinct artifacts evicts the working set within minutes (the planner's figures: 18 GiB in about a minute at 16 anonymous
slots), every request of a legitimate caller turns into a miss, and the transfer network carries the churn and the refills. What bounds it
today: the main installation's per-caller budgets, the Bastion's per-address miss limit and its 16 anonymous slots. What would close it, each waiting for
an answer of the owner in W-34: an eviction that protects what was served twice, a maximum throughput per Bastion, and download budgets per
caller at the Bastion; none of them is built here.

*Decided on 2026-11-26:* the owner chose all three remedies: the cache protects what was served twice
([Q-BAS-333](#q-bas-333--what-was-served-twice-is-protected-in-the-cache), R-BAS-098, package E11), the throughput is capped per Bastion ([Q-BAS-331](#q-bas-331--the-maximum-throughput-is-enforced-at-the-bastion-on-every-byte-it-reads), R-BAS-097, E10), and budgets
per subject apply at the Bastion ([usage-and-limits.md](usage-and-limits.md) Q-LIM-305, R-BAS-096, E9b). *Since E10 (2026-11-26)* the churn
crosses the transfer network at most at the throughput's cap, and anonymous misses at most at its anonymous share (50 MB/s by default);
*until E11 landed* the working set was still evicted as described; *since E9b* each caller's cached and uncached bytes and upstream
requests are bounded by its budget at the Bastion's place, an anonymous one per address (H-2287).

*Narrowed on 2026-11-26 by E11 (R-BAS-098):* a stream of single requests for distinct artifacts no longer evicts what was served twice, as
long as that fits in 80 % of an area; it still crosses the transfer network one fill per request, and the refills of what was served once
before it are misses. An attacker who requests each artifact twice displaces the working set at twice the requests
([H-2290](../security/bastion.md#h-2290--the-protected-markers-are-neither-signed-nor-hard-to-earn)). Measured with the flood of E4 run
again ([developer/bastion.md](../developer/bastion.md#the-flood-again-with-the-protection-of-what-was-served-twice-measured-2026-11-26)): a
warm `npm ci` of 475 packages went from 475 misses during and after the flood to 475 hits. The throughput (E10) and the budgets at the
Bastion (E9b) are built since.

### H-2273 · The bytes between a Bastion and the main installation are counted and not bounded

Stage: R-BAS-090, the forwards of R-BAS-021 and the direct reads of R-BAS-074. Subject: the network between the main installation and a
Bastion, and the main installation's egress, the owner's case of W-34 (2026-11-26).

Live on every Bastion. `quader_bastion_forwarded_bytes_total` and `quader_bastion_fill_bytes_total` show what crosses; nothing bounds it per
Bastion. What bounds it today is per caller and per slot: a forward is the caller's own request at the main installation and charged and
paced against the caller's budget (with the registration's `egress` listing the Bastion's address), and a Bastion holds at most
`bastion.main.max_concurrent` requests to the main installation. Many callers within their budgets, from many addresses, together fill the
network. What would close it: a maximum throughput per Bastion, which waits for the owner's decision in W-34.

*Decided on 2026-11-26:* the owner chose a maximum throughput per Bastion, enforced at the Bastion on every byte it
reads ([Q-BAS-331](#q-bas-331--the-maximum-throughput-is-enforced-at-the-bastion-on-every-byte-it-reads), R-BAS-097, package E10); a taken-over Bastion ignores it
([H-2289](../security/bastion.md#h-2289--a-bastion-that-was-taken-over-ignores-its-throughput-cap)). *Closed by E10 (2026-11-26):* every
Bastion paces what it reads to its registration's throughput, 200 MB/s by default (R-BAS-097). What stays is the Bastion's own honesty
(H-2289) and the replicas' shares without Valkey ([H-2360](../security/bastion.md#h-2360--without-valkey-the-throughputs-replicas-hold-their-shares-as-bastionreplicas-says)).

### H-2274 · The main installation counts no handover, and the Bastion counts only its fills by class

Stage: R-BAS-090. Subject: an operator's view of the bytes between the two sides, not a confidentiality or integrity property.

Live where a registration's handover is on, and on every Bastion for bodies it does not keep. A handover's bytes go from the object store to
the Bastion: the main installation writes an empty body and counts the handover in `quader_storage_download_handovers_total`, not its bytes
in `quader_bastion_forwarded_bytes_total`; the Bastion counts them as `quader_bastion_fill_bytes_total{source="store"}`. A body the Bastion
passes through unkept and a document kept from memory are read from the main installation without a fill: they are in
`quader_bastion_bytes_served_total{source="main"}`, by no class, so the Bastion's own figures by class cover its fills only, and the main
installation's figure is the complete one for what it sent. What makes it real: an operator who adds the Bastion's fill bytes and expects the
main installation's figure.

### H-2275 · The main installation's RateLimit field tells a NuGet or Galaxy client the whole wait

Stage: stage 7 of the main installation (R-LIM-020) on a NuGet or Ansible Galaxy path. Subject: the RateLimit fields of a refusal, not
`Retry-After`.

Live wherever the download limits are in `enforce`. The main installation sets the RateLimit fields on the writer before the format's
`WriteError` renders the refusal (`httplimit.SetPolicies`, `httplimit.SetRefusalPolicy`), and `WriteError` caps `Retry-After` alone: a
NuGet client blocked for 15 minutes reads `Retry-After: 30` and `t=900`. A Bastion's own refusal tells `t=30` (R-BAS-091), so the two
sides differ in `t`. No client of either format reads the RateLimit fields (formats/nuget.md R-NUGET-032 lists what the NuGet clients
read), so nothing waits longer for it. What makes it real: a client of either format that starts to read `t`. What would close it: the
format's `WriteError` rewriting the `t` of the fields it finds to its cap, or the stage setting them through the format's facts.

### H-2276 · The busiest second of an `npm ci` and the requests in flight of a large `dotnet restore` are not measured

Stage: R-BAS-038, the edge's `edgeLimit.requestsPerSecond` and `edgeLimit.connections`. Subject: one address's normal command, refused by
the ingress with a `429` that carries no `Retry-After`.

Live on every Bastion with `edgeLimit.enabled` (the default). The defaults of R-BAS-092 hold the commands of the measurement by their
averages: `npm ci` of 475 packages is about 190 requests a second over 2.5 s, its busiest second not recorded; a `dotnet restore` on Linux
sends with no bound of its own (`maxHttpRequestsPerSource` is `Int32.MaxValue` there, by NuGet's documentation), so a solution with
hundreds of packages may hold more than 256 requests in flight from one address. Neither was run through a Bastion. What makes it real: a
large restore from one address, or several commands of one NAT at once above 1,000 requests a second. The value of either key can be
raised per installation; what would close it is the measurement of W-34's package E4, written on developer/bastion.md.

### H-2277 · Many clients with credentials behind one address are held to one person's figures

Stage: R-BAS-035, the Bastion's own stage, which counts per client address (R-BAS-019). Subject: callers behind one NAT or one CI egress.

Live on every Bastion. The figures with a credential are the main installation's profile Standard, one person's: 200 a second with a burst
of 4,000 and 4,000 misses a minute. Twenty CI jobs that each install 475 packages at once from one egress address (9,500 requests) are
refused beyond the burst, and docker exits at the first `429`; the main installation, which counts per subject, would admit them under
the profile Technical. What makes it real: a company that reaches a Bastion from one egress address for its build fleet. The address can be
listed in the configuration's `limits.flood.exemptNetworks`, which exempts it from every limit, timeout and block; what would close it is limits by subject
at the Bastion, which wait for the owner's decisions of W-34.

*Decided on 2026-11-26:* the owner chose budgets per subject at the Bastion beside the flood protection per address
([usage-and-limits.md](usage-and-limits.md) Q-LIM-305, R-BAS-096, package E9b), and the flood figures per Bastion on its card (R-BAS-093); a
Bastion for a build fleet takes the preset Partner network or a higher `authenticated` figure. The per-address flood figures stay one
person's under the preset Internet. *Today:* live as described; since E9a the figures are the configuration's, since E8 an administrator
sets them on the registration, and since E9b each caller with a credential is also charged its own budget at the Bastion's place, which
does not lift the per-address figures.

### H-2407 · A Bastion's grade in a list says nothing of when and against which database it was checked

Stage: the catalogue's documents of a package's grades per version (`packages/<id>/vulnerabilities`, Q-BAS-403) and of the index, and the
Bastion's grade in the shared lists. Subject: a visitor who wants to judge how current an image's grade is, not a confidentiality or
integrity property.

Live on every Bastion, narrowed by W-36's P8. The main installation's grade names when an image was scanned, by `vuln-scanner-trivy` and
against which database, and its screens compare that database with today's (R-VULN-051, R-VULN-052). The catalogue keeps the time of a
check and the database out of its documents, so that a rescan under a new database changes none of them (Q-VULN-296). On a version's page
the Bastion puts them back from the version's state and compares them with today's database, which the catalogue's state carries since
interface version 11 ([Q-BAS-490](#q-bas-490--todays-signatures-travel-in-the-catalogues-state-without-the-import-the-engine-and-staleness)):
its details say when, by which unit, the database then and today and how current. A list's grade has no state to read them from: the
versions table's and a package list's grade open with the rule and the counts only, as a list's malware mark names no class
([malware-scanning.md](malware-scanning.md) Q-MAL-139). The analyser's version and the time the installation fetched today's database stay
out everywhere (B.15 of W-36's plan). What would close it: the check's time and database of every version in a state of the package (a new
kind of the catalogue's grammar), which a list then reads once.
